subject: social-studies
title: Landscape Change: The Singapore River Mouth, Stage by Stage

segments.say: Stage 1: a fishing village at the river mouth. A few families live in huts and fish from small boats, and the people bar is tiny - very few people live here. Point at the people bar on your student notes before it starts to climb.
questions: What does this place look like at this stage, and what are the people doing?
How many people live here, and how does the bar show it?

segments.say: Stage 2: trade grows and a port is built. More ships come to trade, so godowns are built to store goods and a jetty reaches into the water; more people arrive to work at the port and the people bar climbs. Now try the godown question on your worksheet.
questions: What was built when trade grew, and why?
Why does the people bar climb at this stage?

segments.say: Stage 3: the port expands with steamships. Steamships replace sailing ships, long rows of warehouses are added, and the people bar climbs again as the bigger port offers more work. Check the stage order against your student notes before moving on.
questions: How is this stage different from stage 2?
What made more people arrive at this stage?

segments.say: Stage 4: the modern city, built stage by stage. Tall buildings, busy roads and container ships stand on the same shore, and the people bar is at its highest. Keep the whole order - fishing village, trading port, expanded port, modern city - in view as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
questions: What stands on this shore now?
What is the whole change, in order, with no stage skipped?
segments.watchFor: Singapore's landscape changed in one sudden jump, because the fishing village was replaced by the modern city in a single step. Listen for students who skip the middle stages and jump straight from the village to the city. Send them back to the stage timeline: The change was gradual and driven by growing trade: the fishing village first became a trading port with godowns and a jetty, the port then expanded with warehouses and steamships, and only later did the modern city of tall buildings, roads and container ships rise - stage by stage at the same site, with the population growing at every stage.
